description: defk-9vl case guards: an error inside a guard (i64 overflow, rem/div by zero) raises, while Elixir treats a guard error as the guard failing and tries the next clause. Match Elixir: evaluate guards with flagged ops (defk_*_i64_s overflow flags from defk-jp3, plus a flagged rem/div) and treat a flagged error as false. Add tests comparing with Elixir for overflow and rem-by-zero in guards.

comments.text: Per 'What is the one rule a kernel author keeps in their head?' (defk-dtw.7): a guard error raising instead of failing the clause is a limit (raises where Elixir succeeds): allowed and documented; this ticket stays nice-to-have.

Decision: only genuine Elixir guard errors fail the clause (zero divisor in div/rem//, float inf/NaN). An i64 overflow (and abs of MIN, trunc out of range, MIN div -1) still raises: Elixir has bignums, so failing the clause would silently give a different answer than Elixir, a divergence not a limit (the one rule). Native: guard lowered via guard_expr with two flags, gbad (guard false) and govf (replays the plain guard to raise with the usual message); no flags and no change in C when the guard has no op that can fail. In a speculated select an overflow sets the select flag as before. Elixir mode: guard wrapped in try/rescue ArithmeticError only when it has + - * / div rem, reraising Ops.limit?/1 errors. Known edge: guard with both an overflow and a zero divisor raises (limit) in native; Elixir mode answers by evaluation order.

title: Guard errors should fail the clause, not raise
